title: This Dreamer Comes — a Coat of Many Colours, a Pit, a Bloodied Coat
blocks: Peace to you, brothers and sisters. Today we set foot in the last stretch of Genesis, and the longest single stretch in the whole book — the story of Joseph. Fourteen chapters, walking from a pit all the way to a throne.

But the opening chapter of that story is not about a vision, and it is not about success. It is about how a household came apart. And the text names the reason without flinching: "Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children … His brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, and they hated him."
The most destructive force in a family is very often not the enemy outside the door. It is the favouritism inside the house.

And here is what makes it ache. Jacob himself was that child — the boy his own mother loved best. He had been the favourite, and he had paid for it: twenty years on the run, and a limp to bring home at the end of them. Then he became a father himself, and he did exactly the same thing. So today I want to put one question to you: is there a line running through you that hurt you once, and that you are busy copying out all over again right now?
"Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age, and he made him a tunic of many colors." (Genesis 37:3)

The Hebrew behind "a tunic of many colors" is כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּים, and it means literally a long robe with sleeves, or a long robe with stripes. In 2 Samuel 13 this is the garment worn by the virgin daughters of the king.

The point is not that it was beautiful. The point is what such a garment says. A long-sleeved robe down to the ankles is what a man wears when he does not have to go out and work the fields. The brothers were out there peeling under the sun, and the younger boy stood beside them wearing that.

Brothers and sisters, this is what favouritism actually is: a child does not learn with his ears whether we love him — he learns with his eyes, by watching which way we look first. You can say with your mouth, "I treat you all the same." But that garment will tell the truth on your behalf.

And then this chapter says "hated" three times — the Hebrew שָׂנֵא. Verse 4: "they hated him, and couldn't speak peaceably to him." Verse 5: "they hated him all the more." Verse 8: "They hated him all the more for his dreams and for his words." Each time it is heavier than the time before.

That phrase in verse 4, "couldn't speak peaceably to him", is in the original "they could not speak peace to him" — they could not get so much as a hello out of their mouths. Brothers and sisters, when there is somebody in a household who can no longer say "good morning", that is not a small thing. That is an alarm going off.
And we have to say this honestly too: the chapter does not write Joseph up as a wholly innocent child.

Verse 2: "Joseph brought an evil report of them to their father." The word behind "evil report" is דִּבָּה, which means bad talk, an unfavourable report. A seventeen-year-old, wearing that garment, going to his father to tell tales on his brothers.

Then he dreamed two dreams, and he told them out, every last detail of them. In the first, the sheaves bow down. In the second, even the sun and the moon bow down — his own father and mother among them. And look at how the brothers answer in verse 8; the Hebrew presses the point down with the infinitive absolute: "Will you indeed reign over us? Will you indeed have dominion over us?" The whole tone of it is a sneer.
The dreams came from God — Scripture is perfectly clear about that. But when to tell a dream, and who to tell it to, is a question of wisdom.

Verse 11 carries a sentence that matters enormously: "His brothers envied him, but his father kept this saying in mind." "Kept this saying" is שָׁמַר אֶת־הַדָּבָר in the original — the same idea as Luke 2, where Mary "kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart."

One event, two ways of handling it: the son spoke it out, the father stored it up. Young people, hear this — what God has shown you, keep it in your heart first and let it grow there a while. A vision is in no hurry to prove itself. If it really did come from God, then when the time comes it will stand up by itself.
Why should that coat of many colours have stirred up so much hatred?

The original means literally a long robe with sleeves, or a long robe with stripes, and 2 Samuel 13 tells us that this is what the king's virgin daughters wore. The point is not that it was beautiful; the point is what it stood for. A long-sleeved robe down to the ankles is the clothing of somebody who does not have to go out and work the fields. The brothers were out there peeling under the sun while the younger boy stood next to them dressed in that. So this is what favouritism really is — a child does not learn with his ears whether we love him, he learns with his eyes, by watching which way we look first. You can say with your mouth, "I treat you all the same", and the garment will tell the truth on your behalf. And if you want that to change, begin by changing one arrangement that people can actually see.
Was Joseph entirely innocent in all of this?

The text does not write him up as a wholly innocent child. Verse 2 says that he "brought an evil report of them to their father", and the word there means bad talk, an unfavourable report; a seventeen-year-old, wearing that garment, going to his father to tell tales. Then he dreamed two dreams and told them out in full detail, and in the second one even his parents are bowing down to him. The dreams came from God — Scripture is clear about that; but when to tell a dream and who to tell it to is a question of wisdom. This chapter leaves young people a very good reminder: what God has shown you, keep it in your heart first and let it grow there a while. A vision does not have to be proved in a hurry.
The father "kept this saying in mind" — how does that differ from what the son did?

The expression in the original is the same idea as Luke 2, where Mary "kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart." One event, two ways of handling it: the son spoke it out, the father stored it up. And the contrast is a very practical one — keeping something in the heart is not repression. It is giving the thing time to grow up, and giving yourself a chance to discern whether it really came from God or came out of your own ambition. In practice you can do it like this. Write the impression down, put a date on it, and say nothing for three months. Take it out again after three months; and if it is still there, and clearer than it was, then find one mature person and weigh it together.
2. A Light from the Original: Here I Am, I Am Looking for My Brothers
In verse 13 the father says to Joseph, "Aren't your brothers feeding the flock in Shechem? Come, and I will send you to them." And Joseph says, "Here I am."

"Here I am" is הִנֵּנִי (*hineni*) in the original, literally "behold, I". It is the most solemn answer in the whole Bible: Abraham said it on Mount Moriah, Moses said it in front of the burning bush, Isaiah said it in the vision in the temple — "Here I am. Send me!"
And "I will send you" uses the verb שָׁלַח — the very verb used of God sending Moses.
Brothers and sisters, pull the camera back a little and look at the shot: a father sends the son he loves to the brothers who hate him. And the son says, Here I am.

John's Gospel says, "He came to his own, and those who were his own didn't receive him." And what the Lord Jesus says over and over is "the Father who sent me". This scene is a rehearsal, staged seventeen hundred years early.

And there is one more detail. The place the father sends him to is Shechem — the city of that bloodbath in chapter 34. And the brothers, of all places, have gone back there to pasture the flock. And when Joseph reaches Shechem, they are not there.
Verse 15: "A certain man found him, and behold, he was wandering in the field. The man asked him, 'What are you looking for?'"

"Wandering" is תֹעֶה in the original — the very word of Isaiah 53, "All we like sheep have gone astray." And "What are you looking for" — מַה־תְּבַקֵּשׁ — is the same sentence the Lord Jesus turns round and puts to the disciples in John 1: "What are you looking for?"
And Joseph's answer is the most moving line in the whole chapter: "I am looking for my brothers." (אֶת־אַחַי אָנֹכִי מְבַקֵּשׁ)

He has no idea that they are planning to kill him. All he knows is that his father asked him to go and see whether it was well with his brothers. And when he hears that they have moved on to Dothan, he walks another twenty-odd kilometres.
From the valley of Hebron to Dothan is a hundred kilometres of road. And the whole way along it, the sentence in his heart is this: I am looking for my brothers.

Brothers and sisters, that sentence went on to become the main line of the entire Bible. There is One who set out from heaven and walked a road far longer than that one, and what he says is the same sentence: I have come to look for my brothers.
What weight does "Here I am" carry?

The original is הִנֵּנִי, literally "behold, I". It is the most solemn answer in the Bible: Abraham said it on Mount Moriah, Moses said it in front of the burning bush, Isaiah said it in the vision in the temple — "Here I am. Send me!" And the verb behind "I will send you" is the very one used when God sent Moses. Pull the camera back a little and look at the shot: a father sends the son he loves to the brothers who hate him, and the son says, Here I am. John's Gospel says, "He came to his own, and those who were his own didn't receive him" — and this scene is a rehearsal, staged seventeen hundred years early.
Why is "I am looking for my brothers" the most moving line in the chapter?

Because he has no idea that they are planning to kill him. All he knows is that his father asked him to go and see whether it was well with his brothers; he reaches Shechem and they are not there, he hears that they have moved on to Dothan, and he walks another twenty-odd kilometres. From the valley of Hebron to Dothan is a hundred kilometres, and that one sentence is what he carries the whole way. And the word used of him "wandering" in the field is the very word of Isaiah 53, "All we like sheep have gone astray." That sentence went on to become the main line of the whole Bible: there is One who set out from heaven and walked a far longer road, and he says the same thing — I have come to look for my brothers.
3. There Was No Water in the Pit, and Then They Sat Down to Eat
"They saw him afar off, and before he came near to them, they conspired against him to kill him." (Genesis 37:18)

"Conspired" is וַיִּתְנַכְּלוּ, a Hithpael form meaning to scheme together against somebody, and it occurs only four times in the whole Old Testament. This is not a flash of temper. This is a conspiracy.
They had a nickname for their younger brother: "Behold, this dreamer comes." The Hebrew is בַּעַל הַחֲלֹמוֹת, literally "the master of dreams", and it is said with contempt.
And then comes the second half of verse 20, the sentence that became the theme of the whole book: "We will see what will become of his dreams."

They thought they were cancelling that dream. What they did not know was that every single thing they were about to do was a step in the dream coming true. If you had not sold him down to Egypt, how would he ever have stood in front of Pharaoh? If you had not let a famine drive you down to Egypt, how would the sheaves ever have bowed?
A man may set himself against the word of God. A man cannot cancel the word of God.

In verse 21 the firstborn, Reuben, holds them back for a moment: "Let's not take his life." He says, "Shed no blood", and he says, "lay no hand on him" — and "lay no hand on him" is the same expression the angel used to Abraham in chapter 22: "Don't lay your hand on the boy." What Reuben intended was "to restore him to his father".

We have already watched Reuben lose the birthright. Here in this chapter he tries to make it good — but he only does half of it. He stopped a murder, and he did not take his brother out of there; he left partway through, and by the time he came back the boy was gone.
A kindness that only goes half way saves nobody.

"When Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped Joseph of his tunic, the tunic of many colors that was on him; and they took him, and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty. There was no water in it." (Genesis 37:23–24)
The word for "pit" is בּוֹר, a dry cistern — narrow at the mouth, wide in the belly, smooth down the walls. Fall in and you cannot climb out. Jeremiah was later thrown into one of these.
"The pit was empty. There was no water in it." — that is a redundant sentence. If it was empty, why bother saying that there was no water?
And yet that redundant sentence is the heaviest one in the chapter. It lets us know that he did not drown — he was left down there to die; and it lets us know that down there, he was thirsty.
And then the next verse: "They sat down to eat bread." (וַיֵּשְׁבוּ לֶאֱכָל־לֶחֶם)

Brothers and sisters, that is the coldest sentence in the chapter. In chapter 42 they admit it themselves: "we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen." Which is to say — Joseph was crying out from inside that pit.
They heard him. And then they sat down and ate.

A man can hear somebody crying out and sit down to his meal anyway; and once the conscience has been pushed down, he can go on living twenty perfectly ordinary years. But it does not disappear — twenty years later, standing in front of the granaries of Egypt, that sentence came out of them by itself.

Then Judah makes his proposal: "What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? Come, and let's sell him to the Ishmaelites." The word behind "profit" is בֶּצַע, used specifically of dishonest gain. They sold their own brother for twenty pieces of silver — and Leviticus 27 records that the valuation of a male from five years old to twenty is exactly twenty shekels.
And this line runs on, seventeen hundred years later, into another figure: thirty pieces of silver.

And the goods that caravan of Ishmaelites was carrying were "spices and balm and myrrh". Frankincense and myrrh turn up later in two places: among the gifts of the wise men from the east, and in the graveclothes of the Lord Jesus.
"The pit was empty. There was no water in it" — isn't that sentence simply redundant?

On the face of it, yes: if it was empty, why bother saying that there was no water? And yet that redundant sentence is the heaviest one in the chapter. It tells us two things. He did not drown — he was left down there to die; and down there, he was thirsty. And the very next verse is "They sat down to eat bread." In chapter 42 they admit it themselves: "we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen." Which is to say, Joseph cried out from inside that pit, they heard him, and then they sat down and ate. In two sentences the Bible has finished writing down how cold a human heart is able to get.
The last section of the chapter is a reckoning.

"They took Joseph's tunic, and killed a male goat, and dipped the tunic in the blood. They took the tunic of many colors, and they brought it to their father, and said, 'We have found this. Examine it, now, and see if it is your son's tunic or not.'" (Genesis 37:31–32)
"Examine it, now" is הַכֶּר־נָא in the original. Back in chapter 27, Jacob stood in goatskins in front of his blind father, and the text says of Isaac that he "didn't recognize him" — the same root.
Years ago he used goatskins and his brother's clothes to deceive his father. Today his sons use goat's blood and his son's clothes to deceive him. Even the props are the same.

Brothers and sisters, the Bible does not say that this was God taking revenge. The Bible simply sets the two scenes side by side and lets us look at them for ourselves. Whatever a man sows, that he also reaps — and the harvest very often comes in through the hands of his own children.

Jacob says, "It is my son's tunic. An evil animal has devoured him." The line the brothers wrote back in verse 20 is the line the father now delivers, word for word. They did not even have to tell a lie. They only had to produce the evidence, and their father finished the rest of the story himself.

And then: "Jacob tore his clothes, and put sackcloth on his waist, and mourned for his son many days. All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. He said, 'For I will go down to Sheol to my son, mourning.'" (Genesis 37:34–35)

"Refused to be comforted" is וַיְמָאֵן לְהִתְנַחֵם. Jeremiah 31 uses that same phrase — "Rachel weeping for her children. She refuses to be comforted" — and when Matthew takes it up, he takes it up over the weeping in Bethlehem.
And the word "Sheol" (שְׁאוֹל) makes its first appearance in the Bible right here. It is a father's grief that carries that word into Scripture.
And the children comforting him are the very people who did it to him. From this day on, that household lives with a lie for twenty-two years.

Verse 36 closes it out: "The Midianites sold him into Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh's, the captain of the guard." "Captain of the guard" is שַׂר הַטַּבָּחִים in the original, literally "chief of the slaughterers".
So the last picture in the chapter is this: a seventeen-year-old boy, stripped of his clothes, sold, standing in the house of a man whose title is chief of the slaughterers.
And God does not say a word. From the first verse of this chapter to the last, God never once makes a sound.
But after the first verse of the next chapter, the text will tell us this: "Yahweh was with Joseph." He was there the whole time. He simply was not speaking just then.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
This chapter is so dramatic that it is the easiest of all to preach crooked. There are several places we have to be able to recognise.

The first distortion is preaching Joseph as a wholly innocent victim. He carried tales, and he told his dreams out in every detail. The text is honest, and we have to be honest too. Turn him into a saint and the young people in the room will never learn the very thing this chapter has to teach them — that a vision is kept in the heart first. The test is: when the congregation has heard you, have they learned wisdom, or only pity?

The second distortion is the reverse — using this chapter to reproach the victim: "he brought some of it on himself." Joseph's immaturity and his brothers' murder plot are not remotely the same order of thing. A seventeen-year-old speaking tactlessly does not mean he deserved to be thrown into a pit. Any way of putting it that shifts even a little of the responsibility onto the victim has to be stopped where it stands.

The third distortion is passing lightly over the brothers' evil and saying only that "God meant it for good." In chapter 50 Joseph himself says, "you meant evil against me." Evil is evil. Jumping too quickly to the good God meant is a cruelty to the one who was hurt. The test is: when someone who has been wounded has heard you, does he feel that his wound has been acknowledged?

The fourth distortion is preaching the coat of many colours as nothing but a father's affection. That garment is the starting point of every crack in this family, and the text writes the cause and the effect out plainly. Dress it up and no parent in the room will ever be brought into the light. When the parents have heard you, have they gone and examined their own favouritism?

The fifth distortion is using this chapter to urge people that "if you have a vision you should say it out loud." Mary kept all these things and pondered them in her heart; that is a different sample altogether. Without that discernment you will raise a whole crop of people in a hurry to prove themselves. Has the congregation learned to store things up, or to publicise them?
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: in our families there is very often a favouritism that everybody knows about and nobody names. It might be the one who does well at school; it might be the one who is most like his father; it might be the only son. The elders will not admit it and the younger ones dare not raise it, and so it becomes the thing the whole household walks around. Brothers and sisters, if you are a parent, I am not asking you to beat yourself up. I am asking you to watch one thing this week. Which child do your eyes go to first? Which one do your words praise most often? A coat of many colours is not necessarily a coat — it may be a sentence, a sum of money, a seat at the table. And if you are the child who never got the coat, I want to say this to you: your pain is real, and God has seen it; but you do not have to spend a whole lifetime fighting for that garment, because with your Father in heaven you have had one all along.

The second question: we are far too good at using "look what he did first" to excuse our own coldness. When those brothers sat down to eat, they will have had a whole case assembled inside them — he told tales on us, he loved to show off, he had it coming. And so do we: look how that person once treated me, look how he refuses to pull himself together. And with that, the crying can be ignored. This week I am asking you to answer one person you heard and never answered. You do not have to solve his problem — one message, one phone call is enough. Because the moment we start finding reasons for our own coldness, we are already sitting on the edge of the pit.
There is a line in me that hurt me once and that I am now copying out again. How do I cut it?

Start by looking at Jacob. He was himself the child his mother loved best; he had been favoured, and he had paid for it — twenty years on the run, and a limp — and then he became a father and did exactly the same thing. So cutting that line takes more than simply knowing about it. In practice there are three steps. First, name it: write the thing down as one sentence — "what my father did to me back then is what I am now doing to so-and-so." Second, find one person to be your witness, and ask him to tell you when you are re-enacting it; a line like this is nearly always invisible to the one carrying it. Third, change one concrete action, not one resolution. Resolutions retreat; actions leave a mark.
7. Living 321 Out — Here I Am, I Am Looking for My Brothers
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. The father sent Joseph to go and see his brothers, and he said, "Here I am." Then he walked a hundred kilometres, straight into the most dangerous place there was. And that Father "who sent me" also sent his only Son, to people who would not receive him. My role model is this: he walked obediently into the dangerous place, for no other reason than to look for his brothers.

The Bible is my standard. My feelings tell me, "they are not worth the journey"; the standard says, "I am looking for my brothers." My feelings calculate the risk for me; the standard tells me the mission. When the two of them collide, listen to the standard.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. When to speak out what God has shown you, and who to speak it to, is a matter of guidance, not a matter of zeal. Joseph got the timing of his dreams wrong, and it cost him a great deal. Rely on the intellect and on yourself and you will worry; rely on the heart and on the Holy Spirit and you will be glad. Keep it in your heart first, and wait for the Spirit to open the road.

Let Jesus be King. "We will see what will become of his dreams" — human beings imagining that they can cancel what God has said. Letting Jesus be King means acknowledging that what he says will certainly come to pass: I cannot stop it, I do not need to stop it, and nobody else can stop it either. If you believe that, then you do not have to despair in the pit, and you do not have to be pleased with yourself on the heights.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. When Joseph later stood in front of the throne, what he said was, "It isn't in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace." The dream was God's to give, the fulfilling of it was God's to do, and so of course the glory is God's. It is exactly the same with what God has shown you today — it is not your credential, it is his trust.

Establish God's system. They sold him for twenty shekels — the price of a slave; that caravan of merchants was carrying frankincense and myrrh; and this line runs on all the way to thirty pieces of silver and a cross. To establish God's system is to walk on a line of salvation God laid down long ago. The stretch of road you are walking today is a great deal longer than you think it is.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same Pit
We read this chapter with four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "That could never happen in my family." Jacob thought so too. He had been wounded by favouritism, and he still could not see that he was doing the very same thing — that is pride at its most effective, keeping a man from seeing himself. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, deciding on behalf of the whole household who deserves to be loved; humility is returning to our position as human beings and admitting that I need somebody else to tell me where my blind spot is.

The fearful heart says, "If I say it out loud, this family will fall apart." A great deal of the silence in families is fear. But the silence in this family was kept up for twenty-two years, and the price of it was a father who woke every day believing a wild animal had eaten his son. Fear wants you to keep the thing covered; the Holy Spirit wants you to lift the cover, at the right time, and in love.

The ashamed heart says, "I am the one who sat by the pit and ate." You once heard somebody crying, you did not answer, and you remember it to this day. Brothers and sisters, Judah is the one who later stands up and offers himself as surety for Benjamin; a man who sat by the pit is a man who can change. The gospel is not asking you to stay frozen at the edge of that pit for the rest of your life. It is asking you to get up and walk back.

The wounded heart says, "I am the one who was thrown into the pit." And what makes it hurt more is that the people who threw you in were your own family. I am not going to tell you "God meant it for good" and paper over your pain with it; the text says for itself that they meant to harm him. What I want to tell you is something else. God did not say one word in that chapter — but at the opening of the next one the text writes, "Yahweh was with Joseph." He was already there in the pit. He simply was not making a sound just then.
Four kinds of heart, one and the same pit. And the Lord who was once stripped of his clothes, sold, and handed over by his own people — he knows that pit.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, towards God. Ask God to shine his light on the favouritism in your family — whether you are the one giving it or the one on the receiving end of it. And when the light comes, own it in his presence.
Second, towards yourself. Watch for one week: which person do your eyes go to first? Who gets most of your praise? Write the answer down. You do not have to blame yourself; see it first.
Third, towards people. Answer one person you heard and never answered. Even if it is only a message, only a line that says, "I have been thinking of you." Stop waiting for the right moment.
Fourth, towards daily living. This week, do not use "look what he did first" to excuse your own coldness. Every time that sentence comes up, swap it for a prayer.

Fifth, towards the mission. Take what God has shown you lately and keep it in your heart to grow for a while. Do not be in a hurry to announce it; do not be in a hurry to prove it. When the time comes, the sheaf will stand up by itself.

Sixth, tell it to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First sentence: there is a young man in the Bible who was thrown into a pit by his own brothers and sold. Second sentence: from the beginning of that chapter to the end God does not say a single word, and yet the first line of the next chapter is "Yahweh was with Joseph." Third sentence: so I believe that when it is quiet, it does not mean that God is not there.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that the line which wounded me stops here, with me; I will not copy it out for my children.
I declare that I will no longer sit by the pit and eat; when I hear somebody crying, I will answer.
I declare that nobody can cancel what God has said; I will not scramble to prove myself, I will wait for him to bring it to pass.
I declare that I will say what my Lord said: Here I am, I am going to look for my brothers.
This week I am to "do one thing for the child who has been left out", and my own home is exactly that scene. How do I open my mouth?

Begin with an admission, not with an explanation. Your first sentence can be: "There is something I have been thinking about for a long time — I know you may feel that I favour someone over you." Do not rush to deny it, and do not say "you are imagining things." Second, name one concrete thing: the year you gave such and such to so-and-so, the time you did not speak up for him. An abstract apology carries no weight; a concrete one does. Third, say out loud the one arrangement you are going to change, and then actually do it — for instance, a fixed time once a month with just the two of you. And last, accept that he may not take it well straight away; that is his own digesting, and it needs time.

As this chapter closes, everything looks ruined. The boy is gone; the father refuses to be comforted; the brothers are sitting down to eat with a lie in their mouths; and the young man in the coat of many colours is being led away towards Egypt.

But God is on that road. He is not speaking, and he is there. Twenty-two years later that young man will stand in front of his brothers and say, "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good." He is not saying that those men did him no harm. He is saying this: the harm was real, and God is real too.

So the focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on other people, not on the circumstances. Not I, but Christ. Because into every pit of ours there is One who has gone down first; his clothes were stripped off him too, he was sold by his own people too, and the price they paid for him was thirty pieces of silver. And he came up out of that pit in order to bring us up out of ours, one by one.

May God bless every one of us; may the line that wounds come to a stop in our generation; may we become people who answer when they hear crying, and people who are willing to keep what they have seen in their hearts; and may we go on believing that he is with us on the quietest days, the days that feel most as though God had forgotten us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point of the lesson into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third transformation — without reaching the third, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ A child does not learn with his ears whether we love him; he learns with his eyes, by watching which way we look first. Which situation in your own family does that sentence touch?
2. ★★ "We will see what will become of his dreams" — and every single thing they did became a step in that dream coming true. What does that tell us?
3. ★ The son spoke his dream out; the father stored the saying up. Why is keeping something in the heart not the same as repressing it?
4. ★★ Reuben stopped the murder, and then left partway through. Why does a kindness that only goes half way save nobody?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I am the one wearing the coat), fearful (I am afraid of being laughed at if I tell my dream), ashamed (I once heard the crying and ate my meal anyway), wounded (I am the one who was thrown into the pit). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read "I am looking for my brothers" out loud, and then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there a line in you that hurt you once and that you are now copying out again? Put it into one sentence.
8. ★ Finish it in one sentence: "The pit inside me — when did it happen?"
9. ★★ This week, for whom will you do something that is not half a kindness — not only holding the danger back, but walking him out of it? Say the name out loud.

Leader's reminder: this lesson will lift the lid on favouritism in the family of origin and on the wound of being betrayed. The group leader should speak about his own first. Do not let members comment on one another's relatives, and do not require anyone to forgive on the spot. If someone breaks down, stop and stay with him, and follow up with him privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your household, which visible arrangement is telling the truth on your behalf? Which one will you adjust this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your service, who is the one wearing the coat, and who is the one out in the field under the sun?
12. ★★★ The practice of keeping it in the heart: this week, write down one recent impression, put the date on it, and say nothing about it for now. Say where you are going to write it.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and ask him to tell you this week whenever you start re-enacting that line. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is a seventeen-year-old in the Bible who was thrown into a dry well by his own brothers and sold abroad as a slave. Second, before he was sold he walked a hundred kilometres with only one sentence in his heart — I am looking for my brothers. Third, so the God I believe in is a God who comes looking for people himself. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the line in you that has to be cut, and the one kindness you are going to finish this week. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to keep us from copying out the very thing that wounded us, and to make us people who can get to our feet when we hear somebody crying.
